newsitem.title: USA: NYS Senate says contributions do not buy influence.
newsitem.headline: NYS Senate says contributions do not buy influence.

text.p: The New York State Senate Majority Leader, who is threatening to end apartment rental rules, on Monday defended state Republicans from charges that landlords had used big contributions to sway his policy.

The issue is a vital one for New York City, which has the vast majority of the protected apartments, as well as other cities throughout the state. The Senate Democrats, the minority party, sought to force a Senate committee to release their bill, which would extend the rules for four years.
Joseph Bruno, R-Troy and Senate Majority Leader, forecast the effort would fail and late on Monday, the motion was defeated by a margin of 33 to 27.

The Senate Minority Leader, Martin Connor, in a prepared statement, accused the Republicans, including Gov George Pataki, who has sought to position himself above the fray as the one who might negotiate a solution, of scaring families and letting the issue take over the agenda.

"This kind of hostage-taking, using the expiration data as a doomsday threat, is unconscionable, an awful way to treat middle and working class families, who just want an affordable roof over their heads. It is also an extraordinarily unprofessional way to govern."

The state for the 13th year in a row started its new fiscal year on April 1 without a budget and the battle over rent controls, which expire on June 15 unless extended, could delay the process until then, legislators have said.

Tenant groups have been swift to enter the fray, with one, New York State Tenants and Neighbors, releasing what it said was a breakdown of contributions by landlord political action committees (PACs). Contributions from landlord PACs added up to $884,925 from 1993 to 1996, it said in prepared remarks, saying the Republican Senate Campaign Committee, which is led by Bronx Republican Guy Velella, totaled $430,500.

Velella, whose district's share of rent regulated apartments is 50.2 percent, according to data provided by a Senate source who declined to be named, told reporters in Albany he supported continuing the present laws. The same stand was taken by Nicholas Spano, a Westchester Republican, whose district has 1,750 rent stabilized apartments.
Bruno said his fight to return to a free-market rental system, with protections preserved for the elderly and disabled, was untainted by landlords' contributions.

"With me, contributions don't buy influence and I would also add that about $74,000 was contributed to Democrats, to the minority and to the Assembly by landlords," he told reporters at a news conference in Albany.

Bruno, who has received a few death threats since he proposed returning regulated apartments, about 1.1 million of which are in New York City, to the free-market, responded to questions about a decision by the Assembly and the state Democratic party to stop taking aid from tobacco companies.

Pat Lynch, a spokeswoman for the Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhatttan, said the Assembly had been weighing such a step for about two years and went ahead with it in the wake of a legal settlement by Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group Ltd, which agreed to pay 25 percent of its pre-tax profits for the next quarter of a century to 22 states. The tobacco industry gave about $15,000 over a two-year cycle to the Assembly's coffers, she added.

Senator Roy Goodman, a Manhattan Republican, who along with his Republican colleague, Frank Padavan of Queens, sponsored a Democratic Assembly bill to toughen current protection for tenants, said he voted to release the bill from the Senate committee and bring it to the floor.

"Without rent stabilization, New York will become a city of the very rich and the very poor, with the middle-class praiced out of the market and our communities will suffer as a result," he said, in prepared remarks.
The Senate source said 80.9 percent of the apartments were rent regulated in Goodman's district, with Padavan's district's share put at 38.4 percent.
